segments.title: Opening: Young David's First Lessons in Disappointment

utterances.text: Welcome to David Copperfield Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of one of the great novels in the English language.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be working through the novel chapter by chapter, passage by passage — asking not just what happens, but how Dickens makes it happen, and why it still matters.
Today we're at Creakle's school — Salem House — and we're watching young David encounter, for the first time, what institutional cruelty actually looks like.
With me are three people whose company I've been looking forward to enormously.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who thinks about how great fiction is actually built — the architecture of sentences, the engineering of a single image.
She has a gift, which I find rare and valuable, for making technical craft feel genuinely thrilling.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions that literature depicts — schools, courts, workhouses.
He will not let us aestheticise poverty or injustice, and I mean that as the highest compliment.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read David Copperfield as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She brings the reader's experience — what's funny, what's devastating, what makes you stop and read a sentence twice.
Eleanor — let's begin with you, because something has always struck me about this section of the novel.
Creakle barely exists as a person before he becomes a monster.
He's built out of whispers and rumour before David ever sets eyes on him.
What is Dickens doing there, structurally — and why does it matter how we first encounter someone like Creakle?
It's a brilliant question because what Dickens is doing is something almost cinematic before cinema existed.
He builds the threat before the body arrives.
By the time we actually see Creakle's face — the fiery face, the small deep-set eyes, the thick veins — we've already been primed to read him as dangerous.
But here's what I find extraordinary: Dickens doesn't just use rumour to build dread.
He uses it to lock us inside David's child perspective, where you can't distinguish between what's real and what's been amplified by fear.
That's sophisticated narrative architecture — and it serves a deeply ethical purpose.
We can't step back and judge Creakle coldly because the novel won't let us.
We feel what David feels.
And the whisper is the masterstroke of that.
I first read this at fifteen, and I remember sitting very still at that line — because it was so wrong, so unexpected.
Tyrants shout. Everyone knows that. Except this one.
Let me read it, because it needs to be heard rather than paraphrased.
"he had no voice, but spoke in a whisper"
That's it. Six words. And they're terrifying.
Because a whisper forces you to lean in — you have no choice — and suddenly the power is entirely with him.
He doesn't need volume. The room comes to him.
I take that point, and I don't want to argue with the power of those six words.
But I think we should stay with what else Dickens tells us about Creakle — because the biography is not incidental.
Steerforth provides a rather precise CV: Creakle was a hop dealer in the Borough, went bankrupt, and then appropriated his wife's money.
Dickens gives us the passage directly — let me read it as it stands.
"he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him, right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully"
That is not a portrait of a monster who emerged fully formed.
That is a failed tradesman who found an institution where he could exercise total physical power over people who could not fight back.
The horror isn't psychological. It's structural. The law gave him that power.
James, I think that's exactly right — and those readings aren't in tension, they're reinforcing each other.
The formal choice — locking us in David's perspective, building Creakle through rumour — is also a political choice.
Because powerless children in real schools had no legal recourse and no perspective outside their own terror.
The form enacts the condition.
David can't step outside his fear to analyse Creakle's social biography — and neither, reading him, can we.
Though I'd push back slightly on the idea that sympathy for Creakle is entirely off the table.
He's a failed man performing power. There's something almost pitiable in the whisper — this furious face, these swelling veins, and no voice to back it up.
He has to terrorise children because that's all he has left.
I'd resist that quite firmly, actually.
Sympathy for Creakle is a luxury that David, sitting in that room with a placard on his back, cannot afford — and I'm not sure we should afford it either.
Failed men with institutional power are not pitiable. They're dangerous. History is absolutely full of them.
That disagreement is live and I want to keep it live — but I also want to bring in the other presence in this scene, because Steerforth is already doing something remarkable.
Caroline — the ink-bottle moment.
You've said this is the line that keeps coming back to you — funny on the surface, but chilling underneath.
Can you read it and tell us what you're hearing that a first-time reader probably misses?
It's one of those passages where Dickens is doing three things at once, and most readers catch one and miss two.
The setup alone is extraordinary — Steerforth lights a match from a phosphorus-box specifically to illuminate his own reply.
He is staging himself. At what age? Thirteen?
Here is the passage — and please hear the detail of the price:

"he dipped a match into his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece"
The seven-and-sixpenny. Not 'the ink-bottle.' The seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle.
He knows the price of everything on that mantelpiece.
That's not charm. That's a calculation wearing the costume of charm.
The phosphorus detail is doing the same work as the rumour architecture we discussed with Creakle.
Steerforth literally manufactures his own dramatic lighting.
And the boys sit breathless in the dark afterwards — that's the last line of the passage.
Dickens is constructing Steerforth as a legend through exactly the same mechanism he used to construct Creakle — through the responses of a captive, admiring, terrified audience.
The novel seduces us the same way David is seduced. We are in the dark too.
I want to put a class fact alongside that formal observation, because they belong together.
Creakle never touches Steerforth. That is the central fact of this entire school episode.
And the reason isn't that Steerforth is brave enough to wave an ink-bottle — it's that Steerforth's family has money and consequence.
Eleanor is right that the narrative makes Steerforth irresistible. But we should notice what Dickens is hiding in plain sight.
The legend that David and the boys construct around Steerforth is, in material terms, just wealth being exempted from the rules that punish everyone else.
We find it romantic. Dickens, I think, intends us to eventually find that romantic feeling quite costly.

And that's where I think you're all converging on the same point from different directions — which is that Steerforth's exemption is simultaneously a narrative device, a class fact, and the poison that David drinks at fifteen and can't purge.
The novel is going to make us watch David hero-worship a man the novel itself has quietly indicted from page one.
That's what sitting breathless in the dark costs you.
That's an extraordinary place to pause — and it points us directly toward where we're headed next.
Because if Salem House teaches David that charm can be a form of power, the next figure he encounters teaches him something darker still — that deference can be a form of domination.
We're going to look at Uriah Heep — and the architecture of social hypocrisy that Dickens builds around him.

segments.title: Deep Dive: The Architecture of Social Hypocrisy—Uriah Heep and the Age of Deception

utterances.text: We've been watching young David learn, through pain and disappointment, how the world is not what it presents itself to be.
Now let's ask what happens when that lesson gets a name and a face — specifically, the pale, damp, long-fingered face of Uriah Heep.
Eleanor, you said before we started recording that you wanted to read that description of Mr. Chillip aloud — so let's do that right now.
Why does Dickens need Chillip at all? What is he setting up before we even get to Uriah?
Yes — and the reason I keep returning to Chillip is that Dickens is establishing a baseline, a zero degree of meekness, before he gives us the counterfeit version.
Chillip is genuinely, constitutionally, almost cosmically mild.
And Dickens gives us the measure of it in one extraordinary sentence — listen to this:
'He walked as softly as the Ghost in Hamlet, and more slowly. He carried his head on one side, partly in modest depreciation of himself, partly in modest propitiation of everybody else.'
'Modest propitiation of everybody else' — that is nine words doing the work of a psychology.
There's no calculation in Chillip. He is this way all the way down.
And structurally, Dickens needs that — because the moment Uriah appears, performing the exact same posture, we have an instrument of comparison already built into the reader.
And what makes it comic with Chillip is the completeness of it — Dickens gives us that wonderful line about not being able to throw a word at a mad dog.
He couldn't have thrown a word at a mad dog — only possibly offered half of one, gently.
That's Dickens being playful, but it's also diagnostic.
Chillip cannot be otherwise. He has no mechanism for aggression. He is, as Eleanor says, this way all the way down.
Uriah can stop. That's the horror of it.
I want to add something to that, because the Chillip comparison is doing more social work than it might appear.

Chillip is positioned as genuinely meek partly because he occupies a professional role — the family doctor — that Victorian society expected to be deferential, to know his place in the domestic hierarchy.
What Uriah does is take that same social grammar of deference — the grammar that keeps the lower orders legible and manageable to people like the Wickfields — and weaponise it.
And society has no defence against that, because the grammar itself is never questioned.
Which brings us to Uriah in his full flowering — or perhaps his full unmasking — in the prison scenes.
Caroline, you described something that genuinely unsettled me when we spoke earlier — the idea that Uriah is actually more coherent, more articulate in prison than he ever was outside it.
Can you read us that moment where Uriah addresses David directly — 'I was umble among them that was proud' — and tell me what we're hearing underneath the words?
Yes — and I want to start with the framing, because Dickens is meticulous about it.
David and Traddles are brought to see the prison's model prisoner — Number Twenty Seven reading his hymn book, heads crammed at the little hole in the door to see him.
And then: 'whom should Traddles and I then behold, to our amazement, in this converted Number Twenty Seven, but Uriah Heep!'
That exclamation mark is doing everything. It's comic shock — but also a kind of accusation.
And then Uriah speaks, and listen to the precision of it — here is what he says to David:
'You knew me when, in spite of my follies, I was umble among them that was proud, and meek among them that was violent—you was violent to me yourself, Mr. Copperfield.'
What I hear underneath that is autobiography deployed as testimony — Uriah has learned to narrate himself in the register of the penitent.
But the grammar betrays him. 'Umble among them that was proud' — the old dialect is still there, and it carries the old menace.
What strikes me about that passage is the look Dickens gives us at the same moment — 'a more villainous look I never saw, even on his visage.'
The words are performing penitence. The face is performing nothing — it's stopped performing entirely.
And Dickens lets those two things coexist in the same sentence, which is the real architectural achievement here.
The system only reads the language. It cannot read the face.
And that is Dickens's indictment of a reform system that mistakes the performance for the reformation.
I think that's exactly right — but I want to press a little harder on what 'performance' means here, because I'm not entirely comfortable with that framing.
The model prison system — the separate system, as it was called — genuinely believed that solitary reflection and structured penitence could transform character.
And Uriah has absorbed that belief completely — absorbed its language, its self-presentation, its emotional syntax.
When he says — and this is the line that should stop us:
'I have committed follies, gentlemen, and I ought to bear the consequences without repining.'
— the magistrates hear contrition. And they are not stupid men, or entirely dishonest ones.
The question Dickens is posing is whether the system has produced a man who has learned to speak penitence — or a man who has been remade by learning to speak it.
Those are not the same thing. But they produce the same result.
James, I want to push you on something. Caroline is saying Uriah has become more sophisticated. Eleanor is saying he's mastered the system's grammar.
But you've said something slightly different and slightly darker — that Uriah has been reformed by institutional logic, which is exactly why the institution is damned.
Is that meaningfully different from just saying he's a great con artist? Because those magistrates in the prison scenes seem genuinely delighted — they think it's working.
Yes, I think it's meaningfully different — though I grant you it's a hard distinction to hold onto.
A con artist maintains a private self that knows it is deceiving. The con artist has somewhere to go when the performance ends.
What the passage suggests — and this is what disturbs me most — is that Uriah may no longer have that private self to return to.
The institution has given him a story about himself that he inhabits more completely than any story he had before.
And the magistrates are delighted — yes. Dickens describes them standing there like a 'highly meritorious museum' with Uriah as the prize exhibit.
That is Dickens saying: the institution requires his performance, rewards it, and therefore cannot see it for what it is.
I find James's reading persuasive up to a point — but the villainous look is still there.
Dickens won't let us forget it. That face is the leak in the system — the place where the old Uriah keeps showing through.
And I think that matters for how we read the 'I pity all who ain't brought here' speech — which I would very much like to read now, because it is extraordinary.
This is Uriah at his most — I don't want to say 'magnificent,' but almost:
'I forgive everybody. It would ill become me to bear malice. I freely forgive you, and I hope you'll curb your passions in future.'

'The best wish I could give you, Mr. Copperfield, and give all of you gentlemen, is, that you could be took up and brought here. When I think of my past follies, and my present state, I am sure it would be best for you. I pity all who ain't brought here!'
'I pity all who ain't brought here.' That line is nearly prophetic — and it's perfectly terrifying.
Caroline, you called that line 'nearly prophetic.' Eleanor, you said it's terrifying because Uriah has become unkillable — a perfect construct. James thinks Uriah may actually mean it.
Those are three completely different Uriahs. Who's right — and does it actually matter which one Dickens intended?
I think it matters enormously which one Dickens intended — but I also think Dickens is deliberately keeping all three alive at once.
That's the architectural sophistication of the thing. If we could resolve which Uriah is real, the scene would have less power, not more.
What makes 'I pity all who ain't brought here' so vertiginous is that it functions simultaneously as satire, as horror, and — if James is right — as something uncomfortably close to sincerity.
The system has given Uriah a complete worldview. And a complete worldview is dangerous regardless of whether the person holding it is performing or believing.
I'll say flatly that I think Uriah means it — within his own terms, within the logic the system has given him.
And I want to be careful here, because Eleanor's point about Dickens holding all readings open is correct — and it's also precisely what makes the satire so uncomfortable.
If Uriah is a pure cynic, the magistrates are merely foolish and we can laugh at them and go home.
If Uriah is genuinely reformed — into this — then the magistrates have succeeded, and that is the most damning verdict of all.
James, let me push this toward the end of the segment with Rosa Dartle's accusation — which I think is quietly the most explosive line in this entire arc.
You want that line to indict institutions. Caroline wants it to indict the people who ran them. But does that accusation let Uriah off the hook entirely?
Because if it does — are we just doing what the magistrates are doing? Finding a comfortable story that makes everyone feel better?
Rosa Dartle's accusation is aimed at Mrs. Steerforth, but its reach is much further than that.
She says — and she says it with full theatrical force:
'You, who from his cradle reared him to be what he was, and stunted what he should have been!'
'Stunted what he should have been.' That is the line that haunts me. Not what he became — what he should have been.
And to your question — no, it doesn't let Uriah off the hook, because Dickens is not writing a tract about social determinism.
But it does indict every person and institution that took a human being and gave them only the tools of abasement — and then acted surprised when those tools were turned outward.
And yes — if we say 'Uriah was made this way' and stop there, we are doing exactly what the magistrates do. We are finding the story that is comfortable, that closes the question.
And what Rosa's accusation does that the magistrates never do is refuse comfort entirely.
She's not offering a diagnosis. She's delivering a verdict — to a woman's face.
And the fact that Steerforth is already dead at this point — that the damage is already complete — makes it the most tragic speech in the novel for me.
'Stunted what he should have been.' It's a sentence about what doesn't exist. About the person that was never allowed to be.
I want to connect this back to Chillip, because I think he's the skeleton key here — even if it seems counterintuitive.
Chillip is meek in a way that has cost him nothing — he was simply made that way, and the world accommodated him.
Uriah was made meek by a system that needed him meek — and Rosa is saying the same thing happened to Steerforth, in the opposite direction.
The novel is full of people who were formed — rather than people who formed themselves.
And David, watching all of this, is the one character trying desperately to believe that self-formation is possible.
Which is precisely where Steerforth becomes so dangerous — because he appears to David as exactly the kind of magnificently self-formed person that David most wants to believe in.
We'll turn to that — and to the question of what it costs David to see Steerforth clearly — in the next part of our conversation.

segments.title: Close Reading: Steerforth's Charm—When Narrative Seduction Becomes Betrayal

utterances.text: We've been talking about Uriah Heep's elaborate performance of humility as a weapon — a kind of social armour built from deference.
Now I want to turn to a seduction that works in exactly the opposite direction — not through abasement, but through irresistible elevation.
Eleanor, before we started recording you made a claim that's been unsettling me ever since — that the novel itself betrays us the way Steerforth betrays David.
Can you read us that passage from chapter 35 — 'Of all the times of mine that Time has in his grip' — and show us exactly where Dickens slips the knife in?
Right, so this passage is tiny — three sentences — and that's part of how it works.
Dickens gives you almost nothing, which means the emotional weight falls entirely on the syntax.
Let me read it to you.
"What an idle time! What an insubstantial, happy, foolish time!"
"Of all the times of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly."
Now — that word 'grip.'
Time doesn't hold, or carry, or keep — it grips.
That's a predator's word, buried in what sounds like sweet nostalgia.
The narrator tells you this period was idle and foolish, and then immediately tells you it's the most tender memory he has.
We are being seduced, right here on the page, into feeling that foolishness is the same thing as tenderness.
And that is exactly what Steerforth did to David — made the foolish feel like love.
That reading sends a chill through me every time, because you're right — we're completely inside it before we notice.
But I want to push on something — what makes Steerforth so devastating isn't just the foolishness.
It's that he pays attention.
And I think David is constitutionally undone by anyone who simply looks at him with intensity.
Think of that image in chapter 10 — David leaving in the carrier's cart, and his mother standing at the gate.
"It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child."
That word 'intently' — it's the same quality of gaze.
His mother, Agnes, Steerforth — they all have it.
David melts under that gaze every single time.
I love that, but I want to push back slightly — because not all of those gazes are structurally equivalent.
The frozen image of his mother is tragic precisely because she cannot protect him.
She is held still by her own powerlessness — the cold weather is almost a formal metaphor for what Murdstone has done to her.
That's very different from Steerforth's attention, which is active, chosen, deployed.
The mother's gaze is grief. Steerforth's is strategy.
James, I can already feel you wanting to intervene — because I suspect you'd say we're making all of this too psychological, too personal.
You want to read that Clara passage — 'He naturally loves a certain person, on my account' — not as a woman in love, but as something almost legal.
What's your argument? Because it sounds to me like you're saying the real villain isn't Steerforth at all.
I'll concede the psychology is real — I'm not dismissing it.
But what Dickens is doing in that Clara passage is giving you a woman who has been taught — legally, doctrinally, domestically — to be incapable of self-judgement.
Let me read it, because the language is doing something very precise here.

"He naturally loves a certain person, on my account; and acts solely for a certain person's good. He is better able to judge of it than I am; for I very well know that I am a weak, light, girlish creature, and that he is a firm, grave, serious man."
That phrase 'a certain person' — she won't even name her own son.
She's been so thoroughly managed by Murdstone that she speaks about her own child in the third person, as if naming him would be an act of disloyalty.
Now — in 1849, coverture is still the law.
A married woman has no legal existence separate from her husband. Her property, her earnings, her children — all his.
Clara isn't being naive. She's been trained, by law and by culture, to believe exactly what she says.
Charm, in this novel, runs along the rails of class and legal power.
Steerforth can be charming because he has nothing to lose by it. Murdstone can be stern because the law makes him right.
James, I hear you, and the coverture point is devastating — it explains the machinery.
But there's something in that passage that the legal framework doesn't quite reach.
She says — and this is the line that breaks my heart — 'when I am not, Peggotty, I worry and condemn myself, and feel doubtful of my own heart.'
She has internalised the condemnation so completely that she condemns herself for doubting it.
That's not just legal doctrine — that's a kind of psychological colonisation.
And David is watching it happen, absorbing it. This is where he learns what love looks like.
I'd agree with that entirely — the psychological and the structural aren't rivals here, they're reinforcing.
What's interesting is that Dickens shows you both simultaneously — you feel the mother's anguish and you can read the law in every word she uses.
Eleanor, James has essentially said that your reading and Caroline's romanticise the novel's psychology — that what looks like seduction is really the law failing the poor and powerless.

So let me put it directly: the boy in chapter 15, lying among the hops, keeping that vision of his mother alive to survive the journey — is that a child using his imagination brilliantly, or is it a child with absolutely no other options?
Both, obviously — but I think we need to hold both at the same time rather than collapsing one into the other.
What Dickens does in this passage is describe the imagination as a survival technology, and he does it with extraordinary precision.
Listen to the rhythm here.
"It always kept me company. It was there, among the hops, when I lay down to sleep; it was with me on my waking in the morning; it went before me all day."
Three parallel clauses — night, morning, all day — structured like a liturgy.
The form tells you: this is devotional. This child has made his mother into something sacred in order to keep walking.
Now — James is absolutely right that there's no material resource here, that this child is destitute.
But the form of the novel doesn't let you stop there — it insists you also feel the beauty of what the imagination can do under those conditions.
That's the seduction. We're moved by his resourcefulness, and the novel uses that movement to make us overlook how completely he's been abandoned.
I'll take that — 'survival technology' is exactly right.
What I'd add is that Dickens is meticulous about where the vision fails.
He writes: 'not until I reached that first great aim of my journey, and actually set foot in the town itself, on the sixth day of my flight, did it desert me.'
The imagination sustains him in the wilderness. The moment he reaches society — civility, streets, help — it collapses.
Because the vision was never about his mother — not really. It was about the absence of any social structure willing to catch him.
Right, so let me throw a proper grenade into this.
James says charm is class privilege in disguise. Eleanor says the novel's form makes us complicit.
Caroline, you've suggested something different — that David can't maintain critical distance from anyone who looks at him with enough intensity.
We saw it with his mother, with Steerforth — and I'm thinking now of that extraordinary Agnes passage, where he registers her 'indelible look of regret and wonder.'
Is David actually the problem here? Is he constitutionally incapable of protecting himself?
I think he is — and I think Dickens knows it, and uses it, and doesn't entirely let David off the hook for it.
That Agnes passage is one of the most quietly devastating moments in the book.
David is drunk, chaotic, oblivious — and then suddenly there she is.
Let me read it.
"I see her face now, better than I did then, I dare say, with its indelible look of regret and wonder turned upon me."
'Better than I did then' — because he was too drunk to see it properly.
The older David, narrating, can see the reproach he couldn't face in the moment.
And 'indelible' — that's not a word for a passing impression.
It's a stain. It stays.
So yes — David is a man who is pierced by being seen, every single time.
Whether it's his mother's stillness, Steerforth's deliberate focus, or Agnes's involuntary grief — he cannot process being looked at.
And I think Dickens is showing us that this isn't charming or poetic. It's a wound.
That reading makes me want to reassess what I said earlier — because if David is a wound walking, then the novel's tenderness toward him is also a kind of complicity.
The 'grip' of Time we read earlier — it's not just Time holding those memories.
It's Dickens holding us, the readers, making us feel tenderness for a narrator who, if we're honest, keeps choosing not to see.
Which brings us back to where we started — the charm is not Steerforth's personal gift.
It's a function of what the world has arranged so that certain people can wound others with impunity.
David's susceptibility is real — but it was manufactured. By Murdstone, by the school, by the roads he walked alone at ten years old.

And I think that's the question that haunts the whole novel — whether David ever fully escapes the conditions that shaped him, or whether the tenderness we feel for him is just the seduction completing itself.
We've been talking about David navigating privilege and powerlessness from the inside — his own psychology, his own susceptibility.

In our next segment, we're going to step back and look at the broader landscape — the people at the margins, the atmosphere of the streets and the workhouses, and what it meant simply to survive in Dickens's England.

segments.title: The Margins of Class: Atmosphere and Survival in Dickens's England

utterances.text: We've been talking about Steerforth's charm — that seductive narrative voice that draws David in, and draws us in alongside him.
But charm, in this novel, is a luxury that only some characters can afford.
This segment, we're turning to the margins — the landscapes, the grief, the people the novel places at the edge of the frame.
And I'd argue those margins are where Dickens is doing his most structurally daring work.
Because the usual charge against him is that he's all surface — melodrama, caricature, the broad stroke.
But look at what he does with light and atmosphere when grief enters the novel.

Eleanor, you've made this striking claim that Dickens is essentially doing something proto-modernist — that when the light itself grieves, that's a structural sophistication we usually credit to Woolf or Conrad.
Can you read us that passage from the graveside scene and make the case?
Yes — and this is the passage I keep returning to when people dismiss Dickens as pre-psychological.
The setup is deceptively simple: a child at a burial.
'The day seems different to me from every other day, and the light not of the same colour — of a sadder colour.'
That is not description — that is perception filtered through grief, rendered as external fact.
The light hasn't changed colour — David has.
And Dickens doesn't explain that. He trusts the syntax to carry it.
That is precisely what Woolf will do, fifty years later, with a different kind of theoretical scaffolding.
I don't want to argue with the Woolf comparison, because I think it holds.
But what moves me in that passage is something slightly different — it's the way the liturgy interrupts.
David registers the clergyman's voice as simultaneously 'remote in the open air, and yet distinct and plain.'
That paradox — far away and absolutely clear — is the experience of shock.
You hear things in extremis with that strange precision.
Dickens has caught it absolutely, and I don't think he needed modernism to teach him how.
I want to pull slightly against both of you — not against the quality of the prose, which is undeniable.
But notice where the passage ends.
David looks across the mourners and sees Peggotty — 'that good and faithful servant, whom of all the people upon earth I love the best' — and is certain the Lord will say to her, 'Well done.'
Now: 'good and faithful servant' is New Testament language, the parable of the talents.
It's also the precise language used — in Victorian England — to commend domestic servants in their letters of character reference.
The sacred and the social register collapse together in a way that I find deeply uncomfortable — however beautiful the prose is.
James, that's a sharp challenge — and I want to stay with it.
Is Dickens giving Peggotty genuine dignity in that passage, or is the religious language actually doing the work of keeping her in her place?
James's reading is historically grounded, and I respect it — but I think it misreads the formal function.
This is a child's consciousness narrating a child's grief — the New Testament register isn't Dickens endorsing a class hierarchy.
It's Dickens externalizing, with absolute precision, the only moral vocabulary a Victorian child of David's background would have available.
The passage redeems Peggotty through the highest framework David can access.
I find myself genuinely between you both on this one.
Eleanor's right that the framework is David's, not Dickens's — it's his childish heart making the promise, his certainty.
But James is also right that Peggotty's own interiority — what she is feeling at this graveside — is completely inaccessible to us.
She is seen across the crowd, 'standing apart among the lookers-on.'
She is always apart. And the novel never really crosses that distance.
That is exactly the point I'd push on, and Caroline has put it better than I did.
Dickens withholds interiority at moments of maximum grief — Eleanor describes that as a formal choice.
But the withholding is not symmetrical across classes.
David's interiority is deferred strategically, temporarily — it returns, enriched, in the next chapter.
Peggotty's interiority is withheld permanently. That is a structural fact with a class dimension.
James, let's move from the churchyard to somewhere considerably grimmer.
You've called the Millbank passage — the prison wasteland — reportage rather than purple prose.
That's a strong distinction to draw. Read us the smoke line and defend yourself.
The Millbank stretch in the novel is not invention — Dickens walked that ground, and he walked it as a journalist walks it.
The actual neighbourhood near Millbank Prison in the 1840s was precisely as described — industrial debris, drainage failures, unfinished speculative building.
Listen to the specificity of the inventory — and this is the line I'd ask you to hold onto:
'The clash and glare of sundry fiery Works upon the river-side, arose by night to disturb everything except the heavy and unbroken smoke that poured out of their chimneys.'
The smoke cannot be disturbed. The smoke is permanent. That is a political observation about industrial pollution, not an aesthetic flourish.
I love that line, and I love James's reading of it — but I have to push back on the word 'just.'
Because the syntax of that sentence is doing something aesthetically extraordinary, and I think that matters morally.
'Disturb everything except' — that exception is doing all the structural weight.
The sentence enacts the smoke's imperviousness through its own grammar. That is not reportage. That is art.
But here is my discomfort — when suffering is rendered this beautifully, does the beauty become a kind of anaesthetic?
We admire the sentence and feel, somehow, that the situation has been handled.
I think that's a real tension, and I want to take it seriously rather than dismiss it.
But look at the full texture of that passage — the 'rags of last year's handbills offering rewards for drowned men.'
That detail is not beautiful. It is grotesque, specific, and angry.
The plague pit story that follows — 'a blighting influence seemed to have proceeded from it over the whole place' — that is gothic contamination being used as indictment.
The prose doesn't aestheticize the suffering — it accumulates horror until you can't find it beautiful anymore.
Caroline, you've flagged something that I find genuinely uncomfortable — David using grief as a stage set for his own ambitions.
There's a moment in chapter twenty-four where he's walking by his parents' grave and already imagining the distinguished figure he'll become.
Is Dickens criticising David there, or is he entirely in on it with him?
This is the passage that makes me trust the novel — and also makes me slightly distrust David.
He walks by his parents' grave — his mother, his father — 'by the hour,' lingering.
And then Dickens gives us this line, straight-faced:
'My reflections at these times were always associated with the figure I was to make in life, and the distinguished things I was to do.'
The question is: is that irony? Or is it tender?
I think it is both, and I think that ambivalence is intentional.
Dickens sees David's self-mythologizing clearly — and he is also David, and he can't quite bring himself to condemn it.
The novel's class fantasy runs very deep here, and I think it's worth naming it.
David is orphaned, dispossessed, sent to the blacking warehouse — and yet the novel is structured around his certainty of eventual eminence.
That passage at the graveside ends with a remarkable image — 'as if I had come home to build my castles in the air at a living mother's side.'
'Castles in the air' — it's a phrase that concedes the fantasy is insubstantial, and yet the novel delivers on every single castle.
Whether that is Dickens being honest about wish-fulfilment, or simply enacting it — I find I change my mind on re-reading.
I want to add a craft dimension to what Caroline said about ambivalence — because the free indirect discourse there is doing something very subtle.
The older David narrating can see the younger David's grandiosity — 'the distinguished things I was to do' has a slight absurdist edge when you hear it from a distance of years.
But Dickens doesn't puncture it with irony, because the older David still half-believes it.
That double temporal consciousness — the child dreaming, the adult remembering — is technically very sophisticated.
Eleanor, I want to close this segment on the sharpest challenge I can find for your formalist argument — and it concerns Dora's death.
You've argued that David hearing about it second-hand — through hearsay — is a profound formal choice about how trauma actually arrives.
But isn't there a risk that the most devastating moment in the novel happening off-page is also its most convenient moment — Dora tidied away so Agnes can step forward?
That is a fair challenge, and I won't pretend the two things are entirely separable.
But listen to how Dickens renders David's knowledge of Dora's death — because the language is doing something precise.
'When the Angel of Death alighted there, my child-wife fell asleep — they told me so when I could bear to hear it — on her bosom, with a smile.'
'When I could bear to hear it' — that parenthesis is doing extraordinary work.
David's account is filtered through his own capacity for grief — which is not yet there.
That is a formally honest account of how devastating news actually reaches us — not in real time, but deferred, fragmentary.
Whether that's also convenient for Dickens — yes. I think we have to hold both things.
For me, the trouble is Agnes in that passage — and Eleanor's reading almost elides her.
Dora dies on Agnes's bosom, 'with a smile.' That smile is doing so much narrative work.
It's Dora consenting to her own replacement — or at least, the novel needs us to read it that way.
And Agnes is already being described as 'like a sacred presence in my lonely house' — she's stepping into the stained-glass window before Dora is cold.
Formally sophisticated? Absolutely. But the novel's treatment of Dora is also a little ruthless, and I think women readers have always felt that.
There's a legal dimension here that neither of you has quite reached.
A Victorian wife, in law, was essentially subsumed into her husband's legal identity — she had no separate standing.
Dora is a child-wife — David's own term — and the novel's formal choice to have her die off-page replicates the legal reality: she disappears from the record without agency.
Whether Dickens intended that, I doubt. But the novel enacts it regardless.
Grief, class, erasure — and the question of whether beautiful prose can be both moral instrument and moral evasion simultaneously.
We'll carry some of that tension into our next segment — because Dickens, being Dickens, also makes us laugh.
Coming up: the comic turns in David's journey — and the question of what laughter is actually doing in a novel this preoccupied with longing and loss.

segments.title: Laughter and Longing: Comic Turns in David's Journey of Self-Discovery

utterances.text: We've been talking about class as atmosphere — the way Dickens makes poverty felt rather than described.
But Dickens is also, of course, one of the great comic writers in the language — and comedy in this novel is rarely innocent.
Caroline, you've said Dickens is a writer of ear first — that you can't really understand what he's doing until you hear it aloud.
So let's test that. Can you read us the 'Blood' speech from chapter twenty-seven — and then tell us what you hear that you simply can't get from the page?
Gladly — because this is one of those passages that almost doesn't exist until it's spoken.
The gentleman in question is addressing a dinner table, looking round — Dickens tells us — with an imbecile smile.
'Oh, you know, deuce take it, we can't forego Blood, you know. We must have Blood, you know.'
And then it builds — and this is where you need the voice — into the absolute peroration:
'it's delightful to reflect that they've got Blood in 'em! Myself, I'd rather at any time be knocked down by a man who had got Blood in him, than I'd be picked up by a man who hadn't!'
What you hear, reading it aloud, is the compulsive repetition — 'you know, you know, you know' — which isn't decoration.
It's the sound of a man who needs constant reassurance that his absurdity makes sense.
And what strikes me structurally is that Dickens sets the joke up in the very grammar of the thing.
The parallel construction — 'knocked down by a man who had got Blood,' 'picked up by a man who hadn't' — is perfectly balanced.
But the content is inverted nonsense — and the balance makes the nonsense feel, for a split second, almost reasonable.
That's the seduction. The syntax does the work. The architecture argues the case even as the content collapses.
I'd go further, and perhaps somewhere more uncomfortable.
This man is not a pure absurdist invention — this is an accurate transcription of how aristocratic apologists actually spoke in the mid-nineteenth century.
The 'Blood' doctrine — hereditary virtue, inherited fitness to rule — was a serious ideological position, not a fringe eccentricity.
And the question for me is: when we laugh at this man, are we being invited to feel morally superior — or are we being let off the hook from examining the structures he's defending?
I hear that — but I'd push back slightly.
Ridicule, in Dickens, isn't evasion — it's a form of moral instruction delivered to people who would never sit still for a sermon.
The very extravagance of 'knocked down rather than picked up' doesn't let Blood off the hook — it demolishes the premise so completely that no one can unknow what they've just heard.
James, I want to press you on exactly that question of complicity — because it runs through the dormitory scenes in chapter eight as well.
Eleanor, you've described those moonlit scenes as Dickens painting David's self-deception onto the floor — the physical light as moral geography.
But is the moonlight doing magic, or is it doing cover?
Both — and that's the genius of it.
Look at what Dickens does with the negatives in the passage where David watches the sleeping Steerforth.
'No veiled future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night.'
That's negation as a literary technique — but it doesn't neutralise the image, it conjures it.
By telling us no future was visible, Dickens makes us see exactly the future that wasn't visible — Steerforth's ruin, his footsteps in the wrong garden.
The moonlight is beautiful — and the beauty is the cover. They're inseparable.
And I agree with Eleanor's reading of the technique — I genuinely do.
What troubles me is what the technique is in service of.
Steerforth is a boy of privilege who will later ruin people with far less power than himself — and the novel bathes him, here, in the most gorgeous moonlit prose it can manage.
David tells us he was 'a person of great power' in his eyes — and the prose performs that power even as the older David narrates it from a distance.
Whether that discomfort is the point, or whether we're meant to simply go along for the moonlit ride — I'm genuinely not certain the novel resolves that.
What moves me in the earlier passage — c8:p46 — is the vulnerability of it, which I think complicates both your readings.
Dickens writes that David feigns to laugh when Traddles pretends to see a ghost — he is performing bravery he doesn't feel.

'A certain mysterious feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe.'
That phrase 'steals over me again' — he's writing from decades later, and the feeling still arrives unbidden.
This isn't a child seduced by charisma alone. This is the texture of childhood itself — the awe, the ghost-fear, the feigned courage.
James, you said earlier that if the novel is this compromised, we should ask why it still works — why Micawber still delights us, why those dormitory scenes still move us.
Is Dickens getting away with something — or is the discomfort actually the point?
Dickens is getting away with something — and I think he knows it, and I think that knowingness is precisely what makes the novel endure.
Micawber is a man who has escaped his creditors repeatedly, who has imposed catastrophically on everyone who loved him — and Dickens presents his departure for Australia as a kind of triumph.
Mrs. Micawber's speech at the ship's prow is played for glory — but if you read it as a social historian rather than a romantic, it's a man running away from his debts while his wife cheers him on.
And yet — I'm moved by it. Every time. Which is either Dickens's greatest achievement or his most successful trick.
I want to go to that speech directly — because Caroline and I have been circling it and I think we actually disagree about it in an interesting way.
Mrs. Micawber says — and I'll read it as a piece of machinery rather than performance:
'This country I am come to conquer! Have you honours? Have you riches? Have you posts of profitable pecuniary emolument? Let them be brought forward. They are mine!'
Those three parallel questions — 'Have you honours, have you riches, have you posts' — that's an anaphora working as a confidence trick.
Each question assumes the answer is yes and rushes past before you can doubt it. The rhythm itself enacts the delusion.
I don't entirely dispute the machinery — but I think Eleanor's reading strips out the love, and the love is not incidental.
Mrs. Micawber says 'Mr. Micawber is going to a distant country expressly in order that he may be fully understood and appreciated for the first time.'
That 'for the first time' is heartbreaking — she is a woman who has believed in this man past all evidence, and she still believes.
The anaphora Eleanor hears as delusion I hear as a wife lifting her husband into the person she has always known he could be.
Both are true. That's why it's devastating rather than simply ridiculous.
Last question — and I want all three of you on this.
James has asked whether the novel earns the right to laugh at the 'Blood' gentleman. Eleanor says the comedy is structurally seductive. Caroline says it's moral instruction through ridicule.

So which is it — are we laughing with Dickens at a buffoon, laughing as David at something we should be uncomfortable about, or is Dickens somehow making us do both at once and hoping we don't notice?
Both at once — and he absolutely hopes you don't notice.
The novel keeps offering us exits from discomfort — the joke, the moonlight, the beautiful sentence — and if you take those exits, you've done exactly what David does.
You've allowed charm to do the work that scrutiny should be doing.
And I'd say the discomfort is the architecture, not a flaw in it.
The fact that we're sitting here genuinely uncertain whether to celebrate or interrogate Dickens's comedy — that uncertainty is the novel working on us.
A satire that made us feel purely righteous wouldn't be half as interesting — or half as honest about how seduction actually functions.
For me, the test is always re-reading.
I've read this novel many times, and the 'Blood' speech still makes me laugh — but it also makes me slightly ashamed of laughing.
And the dormitory scene still gives me that feeling Dickens names — that vague solemnity and awe — even knowing what becomes of Steerforth.
If it still does that on the tenth reading, Dickens has done something that goes beyond both craft and critique. He's told the truth about how we actually feel.
Comedy as truth-telling — and truth that costs something to receive.
Which brings us, I think, to the question this novel keeps circling back to: what it actually costs David to become who he becomes.
Redemption, discipline, the work of maturity — and whether that work is as triumphant as the novel wants us to believe.

segments.title: Closing: The Work of Becoming—Redemption, Discipline, and the Cost of Maturity

utterances.text: We've been laughing with David, cringing at his blunders, delighting in the comedy of his early life.
But now I want to turn to the cost of all that becoming—what the novel asks David to pay, and whether it's worth the price.
Eleanor, I want to start with you, and with a line that I think you'd call the philosophical core of the whole novel.
Most readers brush it off as Victorian melodrama, but you've argued it's far more than that.
Can you read it for us and make the case?
It's three sentences, and Dickens stakes everything on them.
The passage reads:
'I wish I had died. I wish I had died then, with that feeling in my heart! I should have been more fit for Heaven than I ever have been since.'
Now—that's not melodrama.
That is Dickens saying: the self that experienced pure, uncomplicated love is irrecoverable.
Growing up doesn't just change you—it cuts you off from a version of yourself that was, in some sense, better.
The wound of maturity is permanent.
And the whole architecture of the novel—the discipline, the second marriage, the eventual wisdom—is built on top of that unhealed place.
I want to resist Eleanor's word 'wound,' because I think it's doing something rather convenient for the novel.
A wound is something the protagonist suffers.
What I see in those three sentences is a crack in the novel's ideology—a moment where the real grief leaks through before Dickens can domesticate it.
The novel wants David to grow, to earn his success, to discipline his undisciplined heart.
But here, for three sentences, the narrating David admits that the whole machinery of self-improvement has cost him something he cannot name or recover.
And then the novel moves on, and David moves on, and we're all meant to move on.
That is not the mark of a novel that has fully reckoned with what it's said.
I think you're both framing this as a problem that needs solving, and I'm not sure it is.
Eleanor says it's a wound. James says it's a crack in the ideology.
But what if Dickens simply means it?
That the wish is true and permanent—not a stage to transcend, not a symptom to diagnose.
I re-read this passage every few years, and it stops me every time.
Not because it's broken, but because it's accurate.
Every adult who has ever mourned an earlier self knows exactly what David is saying.
That's not the human condition being diagnosed—it's the human condition being witnessed.
Caroline, you wanted to read us the books passage—David and his father's library.
Go ahead and read it. But I want to ask you something first.
James has a slightly harder view of what those books are actually doing for David—that imagination may have kept him docile while the warehouse was breaking him.
Is Dickens celebrating something real, or is there a middle-class fantasy being smuggled in?
Let me read it first, and then I'll take James on.
Dickens writes:

'From that blessed little room, Roderick Random, Peregrine Pickle, Humphrey Clinker, Tom Jones, the Vicar of Wakefield, Don Quixote, Gil Blas, and Robinson Crusoe, came out, a glorious host, to keep me company.'
And then:
'They kept alive my fancy, and my hope of something beyond that place and time—and did me no harm.'
Now listen to that list—the names tumble out like a roll call.
There is genuine exhilaration in that prose, and I don't think it's ideological cover—I think it's Dickens remembering what books did for him.
The boy marching around with a boot-tree centre-piece, being Captain Somebody of the Royal British Navy—that's not passivity.
That's the imagination refusing to be crushed.
I don't dispute the exhilaration—the prose is doing exactly what Caroline says.
But 'did me no harm' is a rather pointed phrase.
Dickens is anticipating an objection—and the objection is not merely Victorian propriety about racy novels.
The objection is: what was the boy doing while he was playing at Captain Somebody?
He was not organizing. He was not resisting. He was not asking why a child should be in that situation at all.
The novel's answer is that imagination preserved his inner life, and I believe that—as far as it goes.
But preserved for what? For a respectable career, a good marriage, a settled middle-class life.
The warehouse boys who had no library did not get to become novelists.
That's a fair point about the social structure, but I think it undersells what Dickens is doing craftwise.
The passage doesn't just celebrate reading—it shows us the architecture of self-construction.
David impersonates his favourite characters—he puts the Murdstones into all the bad ones.
That is a child learning narrative—learning that the person who inflicts the suffering can be recast as the villain in a story someone else controls.
The novel is literally showing us where David the narrator comes from.
That seems to me to be something more than middle-class consolation.
James, let's go to Betsey Trotwood's speech about marriage—because I think this is where your argument becomes sharpest.
Eleanor hears it as a kind of radical wisdom—the climax of a novel about ongoing craft.
Caroline hears existential honesty. You hear something much darker.
What are you hearing?
Betsey says:
'Your future is between you two. No one can assist you; you are to work it out for yourselves. This is marriage, Trot.'
Now that is supposed to be wisdom.
And it would be wisdom, if David and Dora were standing on equal ground.
But Dora has no property rights. She has no legal recourse. She cannot leave.
'Work it out for yourselves' means something very different for a woman in 1850 than for a man.
Betsey is essentially telling David to either develop Dora or get used to her deficiencies—and that the whole arrangement is, fundamentally, his to manage.
The novel presents this as tender counsel. I find it rather chilling.
I take James's legal point absolutely—historically, he's right.
But I think Betsey is doing something more subtle than prescribing roles.
Look at what she actually says: 'It will be your duty, and it will be your pleasure too—to estimate her by the qualities she has, and not by the qualities she may not have.'
That is a direct challenge to David's tendency to idealize—to love the idea of a woman rather than the actual woman.
The whole novel has been about David's undisciplined heart. Betsey is telling him to look clearly, finally.
Is it perfect? No. Is it a genuine advance for this particular man? Yes.
I'm with Eleanor on the speech, and I want to add something James's reading excludes.
Betsey ends with: 'Heaven bless you both, in it, for a pair of babes in the wood as you are.'
That phrase—babes in the wood—is not congratulation.
It carries the old fairy tale. Two children, abandoned, who may not survive.
Betsey knows perfectly well what she's sending them into. The warmth is real, and so is the grief underneath it.
That's not ideology. That's a woman who has lived through exactly this kind of marriage offering what comfort she honestly can.
Caroline, I want to end with you and the moonlit bedroom passage—the houseless prayer.
James has agreed with you that it's one of the most honest lines in the book—but he thinks David promptly forgets it, and the novel is designed to help him forget.
Is James right? Does the novel betray its own best moment?
Here's what the passage says:
'I remember how I thought of all the solitary places under the night sky where I had slept, and how I prayed that I never might be houseless any more, and never might forget the houseless.'
That double 'never'—never be houseless, never forget the houseless—that's not one prayer, it's two.
The first is entirely human—please, not that again.
The second is moral—remember that others still are.
Does David forget? In the daily life of the novel, largely yes.
But the prayer is here, recorded, in the narrator's voice—the older David has not forgotten it, because he has written it down.
That is the novel's answer to James—the act of narration itself is the remembering.
I grant that—and it's a better answer than I expected from that passage.
But the novel also concludes with David financially secure, socially established, in a second marriage that functions—and that moonlit prayer is very far behind him.
If the act of writing is the remembering, then the question is: who gets to read it?
The novel was published in serial installments, read aloud in middle-class parlors.
The houseless did not, by and large, read it.
That doesn't destroy Caroline's reading—but it does complicate it considerably.
Can I come back to the spatial architecture of that moonlit passage?
Because I think there's something neither reading accounts for.
Dickens puts David at the top of the house, overlooking the sea, with the moon on the water.
He then brings in the image of the mother walking from Heaven along the shining path.
And then the eye is pulled down—from the sky and sea to the white-curtained bed, the snow-white sheets.
That downward movement—from transcendence to domesticity—is where the conscience is formed.
The spatial architecture creates the moral moment.
That's what Dickens can do that argument cannot do.
I think that's exactly the right note on which to end—Dickens doing something that resists the arguments we bring to it.
We've moved today from the wound of early happiness to the glorious host of books, from Betsey's hard counsel to a moonlit prayer that neither David nor the novel fully keeps.
And we've disagreed about almost all of it—which is, I think, exactly what David Copperfield deserves.
My enormous thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt—three readers who have given this novel the kind of argument it has always been asking for.
And thank you for listening to David Copperfield Unpacked.

The wooden-legged man turned me about so as to exhibit the placard; and having
afforded time for a full survey of it, turned me about again, with my face to
Mr. Creakle, and posted himself at Mr. Creakle’s side. Mr.
Creakle’s face was fiery, and his eyes were small, and deep in his head;
he had thick veins in his forehead, a little nose, and a large chin. He was
bald on the top of his head; and had some thin wet-looking hair that was just
turning grey, brushed across each temple, so that the two sides interlaced on
his forehead. But the circumstance about him which impressed me most, was, that
he had no voice, but spoke in a whisper. The exertion this cost him, or the
consciousness of talking in that feeble way, made his angry face so much more
angry, and his thick veins so much thicker, when he spoke, that I am not
surprised, on looking back, at this peculiarity striking me as his chief one.
‘Now,’ said Mr. Creakle. ‘What’s the report of this
boy?’

I heard all kinds of things about the school and all belonging to it. I heard
that Mr. Creakle had not preferred his claim to being a Tartar without reason;
that he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him,
right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a
trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully. That he knew nothing himself, but the
art of slashing, being more ignorant (J. Steerforth said) than the lowest boy
in the school; that he had been, a good many years ago, a small hop-dealer in
the Borough, and had taken to the schooling business after being bankrupt in
hops, and making away with Mrs. Creakle’s money. With a good deal more of
that sort, which I wondered how they knew.
c8:p47.summary: The boys reveal Creakle's vicious character, his prior bankruptcy as a hop dealer, and his misappropriation of Mrs. Creakle's money.

c8:p49.text:
But the greatest wonder that I heard of Mr. Creakle was, there being one boy in
the school on whom he never ventured to lay a hand, and that boy being J.
Steerforth. Steerforth himself confirmed this when it was stated, and said that
he should like to begin to see him do it. On being asked by a mild boy (not me)
how he would proceed if he did begin to see him do it, he dipped a match into
his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would
commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the
seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece. We sat in the
dark for some time, breathless.
c8:p49.summary: The boys reveal that Creakle has never dared strike Steerforth; Steerforth boasts he would retaliate violently if Creakle tried.

c3:p76.text:
The doctor having been upstairs and come down again, and having satisfied
himself, I suppose, that there was a probability of this unknown lady and
himself having to sit there, face to face, for some hours, laid himself out to
be polite and social. He was the meekest of his sex, the mildest of little men.
He sidled in and out of a room, to take up the less space. He walked as softly
as the Ghost in Hamlet, and more slowly. He carried his head on one side,
partly in modest depreciation of himself, partly in modest propitiation of
everybody else. It is nothing to say that he hadn’t a word to throw at a
dog. He couldn’t have thrown a word at a mad dog. He might have offered
him one gently, or half a one, or a fragment of one; for he spoke as slowly as
he walked; but he wouldn’t have been rude to him, and he couldn’t
have been quick with him, for any earthly consideration.
c3:p76.summary: The doctor, Mr. Chillip, is introduced as the meekest and mildest of men—he sidled into rooms, walked softly like Hamlet's ghost, and spoke so slowly he could barely throw a word to a dog.

Seven in all his purity, Mr. Creakle directed the door of the cell to be

without repining.’ A murmur, partly of gratification at Twenty
Seven’s celestial state of mind, and partly of indignation against the
Contractor who had given him any cause of complaint (a note of which was
immediately made by Mr. Creakle), having subsided, Twenty Seven stood in the
midst of us, as if he felt himself the principal object of merit in a highly
meritorious museum. That we, the neophytes, might have an excess of light
shining upon us all at once, orders were given to let out Twenty Eight.
c63:p53.summary: Uriah skillfully admits the beef is tough but frames bearing it as duty, confesses his follies, and refuses to repine. The magistrates are delighted by his contrition and angered at the contractor. Uriah stands like a prize exhibit, and orders are given to bring out Twenty Eight.
c63:p53.best_quote: I have committed follies, gentlemen, and I ought to bear the consequences without repining

c63:p85.text:
‘But I forgive you, Mr. Copperfield,’ said Uriah, making his
forgiving nature the subject of a most impious and awful parallel, which I
shall not record. ‘I forgive everybody. It would ill become me to bear
malice. I freely forgive you, and I hope you’ll curb your passions in
future. I hope Mr. W. will repent, and Miss W., and all of that sinful lot.
You’ve been visited with affliction, and I hope it may do you good; but
you’d better have come here. Mr. W. had better have come here, and Miss
W. too. The best wish I could give you, Mr. Copperfield, and give all of you
gentlemen, is, that you could be took up and brought here. When I think of my
past follies, and my present state, I am sure it would be best for you. I pity
all who ain’t brought here!’
c63:p85.summary: Uriah forgives David, hopes for the repentance of Micawber and Agnes, and concludes by expressing his fervent wish that all of them—indeed, everyone—be imprisoned and brought to the reformatory system, pitying all who remain free.

c58:p41.text:
‘You, resent his self-will!’ she exclaimed. ‘You, injured by
his haughty temper! You, who opposed to both, when your hair was grey, the
qualities which made both when you gave him birth! YOU, who from his cradle
reared him to be what he was, and stunted what he should have been! Are you
rewarded, now, for your years of trouble?’
c58:p41.summary: Rosa accuses Mrs. Steerforth of opposing her son's self-will while she herself had given him the qualities that led to his ruin, then nursed those same qualities from his infancy, stunting his better nature.
c58:p41.best_quote: You, who from his cradle reared him to be what he was, and stunted what he should have been!

c35:p110.text:
What an idle time! What an insubstantial, happy, foolish time! Of all the times
of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can
smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly.
c35:p110.summary: David reflects that of all moments in his life, this idle, foolish time of love is the one he recalls with greatest tenderness.
c35:p110.best_quote: Of all the times of mine that Time has in his grip, there is none that in one retrospect I can smile at half so much, and think of half so tenderly.

c10:p156.text:
I was in the carrier’s cart when I heard her calling to me. I looked out,
and she stood at the garden-gate alone, holding her baby up in her arms for me
to see. It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of
her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child.
c10:p156.summary: David's mother stands at the garden gate holding the baby up for him to see one last time as he departs.
c10:p156.best_quote: It was cold still weather; and not a hair of her head, nor a fold of her dress, was stirred, as she looked intently at me, holding up her child.

c10:p89.text:
‘No, Peggotty,’ returned my mother, ‘but you insinuated.
That’s what I told you just now. That’s the worst of you. You WILL
insinuate. I said, at the moment, that I understood you, and you see I did.
When you talk of Mr. Murdstone’s good intentions, and pretend to slight
them (for I don’t believe you really do, in your heart, Peggotty), you
must be as well convinced as I am how good they are, and how they actuate him
in everything. If he seems to have been at all stern with a certain person,
Peggotty—you understand, and so I am sure does Davy, that I am not
alluding to anybody present—it is solely because he is satisfied that it
is for a certain person’s benefit. He naturally loves a certain person,
on my account; and acts solely for a certain person’s good. He is better
able to judge of it than I am; for I very well know that I am a weak, light,
girlish creature, and that he is a firm, grave, serious man. And he
takes,’ said my mother, with the tears which were engendered in her
affectionate nature, stealing down her face, ‘he takes great pains with
me; and I ought to be very thankful to him, and very submissive to him even in
my thoughts; and when I am not, Peggotty, I worry and condemn myself, and feel
doubtful of my own heart, and don’t know what to do.’
c10:p89.summary: Clara delivers an elaborate justification of Mr. Murdstone's stern discipline, portraying him as acting purely for David's benefit and her own good, while describing herself as weak and light.

He naturally loves a certain person, on my account; and acts solely for a certain person's good. He is better able to judge of it than I am; for I very well know that I am a weak, light, girlish creature, and that he is a firm, grave, serious man.

c15:p60.text:
This adventure frightened me so, that, afterwards, when I saw any of these
people coming, I turned back until I could find a hiding-place, where I
remained until they had gone out of sight; which happened so often, that I was
very seriously delayed. But under this difficulty, as under all the other
difficulties of my journey, I seemed to be sustained and led on by my fanciful
picture of my mother in her youth, before I came into the world. It always kept
me company. It was there, among the hops, when I lay down to sleep; it was with
me on my waking in the morning; it went before me all day. I have associated
it, ever since, with the sunny street of Canterbury, dozing as it were in the
hot light; and with the sight of its old houses and gateways, and the stately,
grey Cathedral, with the rooks sailing round the towers. When I came, at last,
upon the bare, wide downs near Dover, it relieved the solitary aspect of the
scene with hope; and not until I reached that first great aim of my journey,
and actually set foot in the town itself, on the sixth day of my flight, did it
desert me. But then, strange to say, when I stood with my ragged shoes, and my
dusty, sunburnt, half-clothed figure, in the place so long desired, it seemed
to vanish like a dream, and to leave me helpless and dispirited.
c15:p60.summary: David's encounter with the tinker traumatizes him so profoundly that he hides whenever he sees trampers, severely delaying his journey. His vision of his mother—young, weeping, and relenting—sustains him throughout Kent and into Dover, associated with the sunny streets of Canterbury and the grey Cathedral. However, when he reaches Dover itself, the vision vanishes, leaving him helpless and dispirited.
c15:p60.best_quote: It always kept me company. It was there, among the hops, when I lay down to sleep; it was with me on my waking in the morning; it went before me all day.

c26:p38.text:
On somebody’s motion, we resolved to go downstairs to the dress-boxes,
where the ladies were. A gentleman lounging, full dressed, on a sofa, with an
opera-glass in his hand, passed before my view, and also my own figure at full
length in a glass. Then I was being ushered into one of these boxes, and found
myself saying something as I sat down, and people about me crying
‘Silence!’ to somebody, and ladies casting indignant glances at me,
and—what! yes!—Agnes, sitting on the seat before me, in the same
box, with a lady and gentleman beside her, whom I didn’t know. I see her
face now, better than I did then, I dare say, with its indelible look of regret
and wonder turned upon me.
c26:p38.summary: David is ushered into a box where he is dismayed to discover Agnes Wickfield seated before him, regarding him with a look of regret and wonder.
c26:p38.best_quote: Then I was being ushered into one of these boxes, and found myself saying something as I sat down, and people about me crying 'Silence!' to somebody, and ladies casting indignant glances at me, and—what! yes!—Agnes, sitting on the seat before me, in the same box, with a lady and gentleman beside her, whom I didn't know. I see her face now, better than I did then, I dare say, with its indelible look of regret and wonder turned upon me.

c11:p87.text:
We stand around the grave. The day seems different to me from every other day,
and the light not of the same colour—of a sadder colour. Now there is a
solemn hush, which we have brought from home with what is resting in the mould;
and while we stand bareheaded, I hear the voice of the clergyman, sounding
remote in the open air, and yet distinct and plain, saying: ‘I am the
Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord!’ Then I hear sobs; and,
standing apart among the lookers-on, I see that good and faithful servant, whom
of all the people upon earth I love the best, and unto whom my childish heart
is certain that the Lord will one day say: ‘Well done.’
c11:p87.summary: At the graveside, David hears the burial service and sees Peggotty among the mourners, feeling certain of her spiritual worth and salvation.
